title: Dealcraft
description: Seven rounds of a high-stakes commercial negotiation: prep, opening offers, BATNA pressure, concessions, a multi-party table, an ethics checkpoint, and the close. Every choice trades off cash, reputation, skill growth, energy, and integrity.
learning_objectives: Distinguish value-claiming from value-creating moves in a negotiation
Manage the tradeoff between short-term cash and long-term reputation
Recognize when an ethical shortcut compounds into a bigger downside

rounds.title: Preparation map
rounds.prompt: Before you sit at the table, how do you spend your prep time?

choices.label: Map interests
choices.feedback: Mapping both sides' underlying interests (not just positions) gives you options to trade later — the foundation of value creation.

choices.label: Model the numbers
choices.feedback: A tight financial model sharpens your anchor and your walk-away point, but numbers alone miss the relationship side of the deal.

choices.label: Call the supplier
choices.feedback: An early informal call builds trust before the formal ask — reputation compounds even when it doesn't show up on this quarter's ledger.

choices.label: Draft a bold ask
choices.feedback: Skipping prep to draft an aggressive ask can work once, but you're negotiating on assumptions instead of information.

rounds.title: First offer
rounds.prompt: It's time to make the opening move. What's your first offer?

choices.label: Justified anchor
choices.feedback: An ambitious anchor backed by visible logic sets the frame without burning trust — the other side can push back on the numbers, not on you.

choices.label: Open extremely low
choices.feedback: An unreasonable opener can anchor hard, but it signals bad faith — expect the other side to harden their own position in response.

choices.label: Invite their proposal
choices.feedback: Letting them anchor first gives up some leverage, but the information you learn about their priorities is often worth more.

choices.label: Offer a range
choices.feedback: A range signals flexibility while still anchoring on the high end — a middle path between an aggressive number and no number at all.

rounds.title: BATNA test
rounds.prompt: The other side is testing whether you actually have alternatives. How do you respond?

choices.label: Validate the backup
choices.feedback: Confirming your BATNA is real (not just assumed) before you lean on it is the single habit that separates prepared negotiators from bluffers.

choices.label: Signal alternatives
choices.feedback: A calm, factual mention of other options applies pressure without a confrontation.

choices.label: Bluff a better deal
choices.feedback: A bluff that gets called doesn't just cost this deal — it costs every future deal with anyone who hears about it. The integrity hit here is the real price.

choices.label: Share switching concerns
choices.feedback: Naming your real hesitation invites them to solve it with you instead of against you — slower, but it usually holds up better.

rounds.title: Concession design
rounds.prompt: You need to move off your opening position. How do you concede?

choices.label: Trade, do not give
choices.feedback: Every concession paired with an ask of your own teaches the other side that nothing here is free — and keeps the deal moving toward a real trade.

choices.label: Hold the line
choices.feedback: Refusing to move protects the number this round, but a negotiation with zero concessions from you risks reading as bad-faith stonewalling.

choices.label: Split the pain
choices.feedback: Meeting in the middle costs you cash this round but is often the fastest way to preserve a relationship you'll need again.

choices.label: Delay the issue
choices.feedback: Punting on a hard issue doesn't make it go away — it usually resurfaces later, at a worse moment, with less goodwill left to spend on it.

rounds.title: Multi-party table
rounds.prompt: A third stakeholder just joined the table with their own agenda. What's your move?

choices.label: Create workstreams
choices.feedback: Splitting a multi-party deal into parallel workstreams keeps every stakeholder's issue moving without letting one blocker stall the whole table.

choices.label: Escalate to executives
choices.feedback: Escalating can break a logjam fast, but it also signals you couldn't resolve this at your own level — use it sparingly.

choices.label: Host joint workshop
choices.feedback: Getting everyone in one room to align on shared goals costs time and energy, but it's often the only way a genuinely three-way deal actually closes.

choices.label: Negotiate privately
choices.feedback: Side-channel deals can be efficient, but they erode trust with whoever finds out they were cut out of the room.

rounds.title: Ethics checkpoint
rounds.prompt: You just noticed the other side's numbers contain an error that works heavily in your favor. What do you do?

choices.label: Disclose the error
choices.feedback: Flagging their error costs you the windfall, but a reputation for not exploiting mistakes is worth more than any single deal — people remember who they can trust with the numbers.

choices.label: Ask clarifying questions
choices.feedback: Asking a question that lets them catch their own mistake is a middle path — you're not exploiting it, but you're also not doing their job for them.

choices.label: Ignore it
choices.feedback: Quietly banking someone else's mistake is the biggest single integrity hit in this negotiation — and errors like this have a way of surfacing after the ink is dry.

choices.label: Ask legal privately
choices.feedback: Routing the question through legal protects you procedurally, though it's slower and less direct than raising it at the table.

rounds.title: Close the deal
rounds.prompt: Everything is on the table. How do you bring this home?

choices.label: Close with a package
choices.feedback: Bundling every open item into one final package lets both sides see the whole trade at once — usually the cleanest way to get to yes.

choices.label: Use deadline pressure
choices.feedback: An artificial deadline can force a decision, but it also forces it under duress — watch for buyer's remorse and a colder relationship afterward.

choices.label: Close a pilot
choices.feedback: Scaling down to a pilot leaves cash on the table now, but it's a low-risk way to prove the relationship before either side commits fully.

choices.label: Celebrate jointly
choices.feedback: Marking the close together — not just signing and leaving — is what turns a one-off transaction into the start of a relationship.

reflection_prompt: Where did you create value before claiming it? Which concession protected the relationship best?
